log.why: E5 tests lacZ and katG together (0.460 probability), giving the most balanced binary split on the shorter-deadline ticket.
Treating at 3 uM splits the posterior mass most evenly (0.593 vs 0.407) while Ticket 1 already has a plate growing.
Ticket 1 has less time left and E1 directly tests the leading candidate katG against lacZ.
Treating at 10 uM cleanly splits the 0.510 posterior mass at or below 10 uM from the 0.490 mass above it.
Ticket 1 has the least time left and lacZ leads at 0.751; E0 directly tests lacZ to push confidence above 0.97 before publishing.
Ticket 2 has 59 s left and 0.247 mass at 3 uM or below; E3 best tests 10 uM against lower thresholds.
Ticket 1 has a 0.971 posterior for lacZ with only 31 s remaining, so publishing now maximizes score.
Ticket 3 has 49s left; E7 splits the posterior cleanly (0.456 vs 0.544) for maximum information gain.
E11 splits Ticket 4 nearly evenly (0.506 vs 0.494) and separates top candidates recA and metJ while overlapping incubation.
Ticket 2 has 10 s left with 0.841 posterior on 10 uM, so publishing now avoids expiration and captures strong expected points.
Ticket 3 expires in 19s; testing fliC (E3) separates fliC (0.358) from gyrA (0.559) to >82% posterior with time to publish.
Ticket 4 has 38 s left and metJ leads at 0.527; testing E5 maximally splits the posterior while Ticket 3's E3 finishes incubating.
Ticket 4 has 20 s left; testing dnaK (0.479) gives the highest information gain and resolves the lead before publishing.
E4 (10 µM) splits Ticket 6's posterior 0.582 vs 0.418 for maximum information gain while E1 finishes on Ticket 4.
Testing 30 uM on Ticket 6 splits the leading 30 uM hypothesis from 100-300 uM before publishing.
Ticket 6 max posterior is only 0.433, and E5 finishes in 6 s, giving time to publish with much higher confidence.
